c.tagline: Where West African beaches meet a laid-back francophone capital.

taxi.fareNote: No meters; agree on the fare with the driver before departing. Shared taxis run fixed routes for 200-300 FCFA; private hire (course) costs more, roughly 1,000-2,000 FCFA within the city.

emergency.note: Fire brigade: 118. Emergency response can be slow; for serious issues contact your hotel, embassy, or a private clinic directly.

avoid.reason: Petty crime; caution on the beach and at night

hood_desc: Lomé's palm-lined beach strip near the Ghanaian border, packed with seaside restaurants, bars and the city's top hotels; suits travelers who want easy beach access and nightlife.

The bustling historic downtown around the Grand Marché, with the Radisson Blu tower, colonial-era streets and the Ewe fabric and bead market; suits first-time visitors who want to be near sights and shopping.
A quieter, leafy residential district minutes from the airport, home to embassies, ministries and the main hospital; suits business travelers and those with early flights.
A sprawling northern suburb of everyday local life, popular with long-stay expats and volunteers for its cheaper furnished apartments; suits budget travelers wanting an authentic, non-touristy base.
A traditional Ewe lagoon-side quarter near the famous Akodessewa Fetish Market, rich in local culture and voodoo heritage; suits culturally curious travelers seeking an offbeat, low-key stay.

water.note: Tap water is not recommended for visitors; use bottled or treated water.

transit.pay: Pay the driver or conductor in cash (XOF) when boarding SOTRAL buses; fares are flat per route, typically 100-200 FCFA. SOTRAL has been rolling out digital ticketing (prepaid cards/mobile payment) since the mid-2020s. Zemidjan motorcycle taxis and shared taxis are paid in cash, negotiated before the ride.
transit.hours: SOTRAL buses run roughly 6:00-20:00; after dark, zemidjans, taxis and the Gozem app are the main options.
transit.note: Zemidjan (motorcycle taxi) and shared taxis remain the most common way to get around Lomé; always agree the price before setting off.

bus: Rakieta Transport (regional coaches to Ouagadougou, Niamey)
Shared bush taxis/minibuses (gbaka) to regional towns and neighboring countries

airport.name: Lomé–Tokoin International Airport (Gnassingbé Eyadéma International Airport) – LFW

transit.m: Negotiated taxi (shared or private) to downtown

tip.r: Not obligatory; 5-10% is appreciated at upscale restaurants and hotels, rounding up is common for taxis/zemidjans.

landmarks: Independence Monument
This soaring 1960s monument commemorating Togo's independence stands proudly in the capital, symbolizing the nation's liberation and enduring pride.
Grand Marché de Lomé
A vibrant multi-story market ruled largely by Togo's legendary 'Nana Benz' fabric traders, packed with wax-print textiles, crafts and West African energy.
Akodessewa Fetish Market
The world's largest voodoo market displays rows of animal skulls, talismans and traditional healing objects, a startling and unforgettable window into West African spirituality.
Cathédrale du Sacré-Cœur de Lomé
This elegant red-and-white striped Catholic cathedral, built in 1902, is one of Lomé's most photogenic colonial-era landmarks near the Grand Marché.
Lomé Beach
Palm-fringed sands along the Gulf of Guinea offer sunset strolls, fishing pirogues and beachside bars where locals and visitors unwind by the Atlantic.
Palais de Lomé
A restored former colonial governor's residence turned cultural center and botanical garden, blending striking architecture with contemporary African art exhibitions.
Lomé Grand Marché Textile District
Beyond the main market halls, narrow lanes overflow with vivid Dutch wax prints and kente cloth, showcasing Togo's storied textile trading legacy.
National Museum of Togo
A modest but insightful museum tracing Togo's pre-colonial kingdoms, German and French colonial history, and path to independence through artifacts and photographs.
Wharf Français (Old Colonial Pier)
The crumbling remains of a German-era jetty jutting into the Gulf of Guinea evoke Lomé's colonial past against a dramatic ocean backdrop.
Lomé Central Station (Gare de Lomé)
This historic railway station, dating to the German colonial period, showcases handsome period architecture and remains a nostalgic symbol of the city's transport history.

train.note: Togo has no passenger rail service - the surviving lines carry freight (phosphate and clinker) only. All intercity and cross-border travel is by road, so use long-distance coaches or shared bush taxis instead. The nearest passenger trains are far away in Ghana/elsewhere.

bus.note: Coaches run the coastal corridor west to Accra (Ghana) and east to Cotonou and Lagos, plus inland to Burkina Faso and Cote d'Ivoire; several Ghanaian and Togolese lines (e.g. STC, STM Transport) also serve Accra. Carry your passport and ECOWAS/visa documents for each border and allow time for slow crossings.

ferry.note: There are no scheduled passenger ferries - the Port of Lome is a cargo and container port. Travel along the coast is by road.
